action-plan.def: A structured strategy for addressing security issues including vulnerabilities, findings, and compliance gaps. Action plans group related remediation items, define priorities and timelines, and assign ownership.

access-to-personal-information.def: The ability to view personal information held by an organization. This ability may be complemented by an ability to update or correct the information. Access defines the intersection of identity and data, that is, who can do what to which data.

american-institute-of-certified-public-a.term: American Institute of Certified Public Accountants (AICPA)
american-institute-of-certified-public-a.def: The governing body that establishes the standards, criteria, and guidance for all SOC 2 Audits. All official SOC 2 reports must be issued by a licensed CPA firm that is accredited by the AICPA.

api-token.def: An organization-scoped credential for programmatic access. Unlike a personal access token, an API token belongs to the organization rather than an individual, so automation built on it keeps working when people leave.

architecture.def: The design of the structure of a system, including logical components, and the logical interrelationships of computers, operating systems, networks, or other elements, whether internally or externally hosted.

assessment-boundary.def: The defined scope an assessment applies to: the people, processes, technologies, data, and facilities under evaluation.

assessment-object.def: The specific item an assessment method is applied to during an assessment, such as a specification, a mechanism, an activity, or an individual.

audit-scoping.def: Audit scoping refers to determining the bounds of the audit, including the time frame and activities that will be covered by the audit.

automated-evidence.def: Automated Evidence refers to data that has been collected from systems through an automated technical solution, rather than manually pulled.

authentication.def: The process of verifying the identity or other attributes claimed by or assumed of an entity (user, process, or device) or to verify the source and integrity of data.

authorization.def: The process of granting access privileges to a user, program, or process by a person that has the authority to grant such access.

asset.def: A resource that an organization owns, operates, or relies upon that requires protection and management. Assets are foundational to vulnerability management and compliance tracking.

assessment.def: A structured questionnaire or evaluation used to collect information about security practices, compliance status, or risk factors. In Openlane, assessments support vendor due diligence, periodic reviews, internal compliance checks, and risk assessments.

availability.def: One of the Trust Services Criteria established by the AICPA, Availability means that the system is accessible and usable for agreed-upon use. Risk example: A denial of service attack brings your service unexpectedly offline.

board-of-directors.def: Individuals with responsibility for overseeing the strategic direction of the entity and the obligations related to the accountability of the entity.

business-partner.def: An individual or business (and its employees), other than a vendor, that has some degree of involvement with the entity's business dealings or agrees to cooperate, to any degree, with the entity (for example, a computer manufacturer who works with another comp…

business-to-business.def: Businesses that sell goods or services to other businesses, rather than to individual users.

business-to-consumer.def: Businesses that sell goods or services to individual customers, rather than to other businesses.

campaign.def: A coordinated outreach effort that sends a questionnaire, attestation, or assessment to a defined set of recipients and tracks each recipient's completion individually.

california-consumer-privacy-act.def: A state statute passed in 2018 that gives California residents new data privacy rights and requires compliance obligations from any for-profit entity that does business with California residents.

cloud-security-compliance.def: Cloud security compliance includes a number of potential frameworks that typically fit into two distinct categories: 1. Compliance centric, 2. security centric.

collection.def: The process of obtaining personal information from the individual directly (for example, through the individual’s submission of an internet form or a registration form) or from another party, such as a business partner.

commitments.def: Declarations made by management to customers regarding the performance of one or more systems that provide services or products.

carve-out-method.def: A method of handling the services provided by a subservice organization in a SOC 2 report.

compensating-control.def: An alternative control implemented in place of a required control that cannot be met as stated, providing equivalent or comparable protection.

complementary-user-entity-controls.def: Controls that reside at the user entity level of a service organization; user entities are the organizations that use the service organization's services.

compliance-framework.def: Part of a Compliance program, a Compliance framework lays out the strategies an organization uses to ensure that it remains in Compliance with both internal and external regulations.

compliance-program.def: A Compliance Program outlines a company’s ongoing and future processes and activities to address Compliance requirements in order to support growth.

compliance.def: The act of implementing, monitoring, and providing evidence for controls that meet established guidelines such as SOC 2, GDPR, or ISO 27001.

compromise.def: Refers to a loss of confidentiality, integrity, or availability of information, including any resultant impairment of (1) processing integrity or availability of systems or (2) the integrity or availability of system inputs or outputs.

confidentiality.def: One of the Trust Services Criteria established by the AICPA, Confidentiality means that only the right people can access the information held by the organization. Risk example: Criminals get hold of your clients’ login details and sell them.

conformity-assessment.def: The process of demonstrating that specified requirements are fulfilled, such as certification against ISO 27001 or an accredited SOC 2 examination.

contacts.def: Contacts are external people your organization corresponds with as part of its compliance program: the security lead at a vendor, the point of contact at a subprocessor, or the recipient of a questionnaire campaign.

control-inheritance.def: When a system receives protection from controls that are developed, implemented, assessed, and monitored by a party other than the team responsible for the system itself.

control-implementation.def: The record of how a control is actually satisfied in a specific environment: the tooling, configuration, and process behind the control's framework-aligned language.

controls.def: Policies and procedures that are part of the entity’s system of internal control. The objective of an entity’s system of internal control is to provide reasonable assurance that principal system objectives are achieved.

control-activity.def: An action established through policies and procedures that help ensure that management’s directives to mitigate risks to the achievement of objectives are carried out.

controls-convergence.def: With the growing amount of frameworks organizations adopt, all of which are focused in some way on security, most controls overlap with controls of other frameworks. There are two ways to address this reality;

committee-of-sponsoring-organizations-of.term: Committee of Sponsoring Organizations of the Treadway Commission (COSO)
committee-of-sponsoring-organizations-of.def: A joint initiative of five private-sector organizations and is dedicated to providing thought leadership through the development of frameworks and guidance on enterprise risk management, internal control, and fraud deterrence. (See www.coso.org.)

common-vulnerabilities-and-exposures.def: A standardized identifier for publicly known cybersecurity vulnerabilities. CVE IDs follow the format CVE-YEAR-NUMBER (e.g., CVE-2024-12345) and are maintained by MITRE Corporation.

common-vulnerability-scoring-system.def: An open standard for assessing the severity of computer system security vulnerabilities. CVSS provides a numerical score from 0 to 10, with higher scores indicating more severe vulnerabilities.

custom-enum.def: An organization-defined list of controlled values for a field, used where consistent categorization matters more than free-form flexibility: the same environments, criticality levels, and classifications appear everywhere they are used.

custom-tag.def: A free-form label applied to records for filtering and grouping. Tags trade the consistency of enums for flexibility, which suits ad hoc groupings that do not warrant a controlled value list. See custom data.

design.def: As used in the COSO definition of internal control, the internal control system design is intended to provide reasonable assurance of the achievement of an entity’s objectives.

directory-sync.def: Automatic population of a workforce roster from an identity provider, so personnel records track the directory instead of being maintained by hand.

disclosure.def: The provision of access to or the release, transfer, or divulging in any other manner of information outside the entity holding the information. Disclosure is often used interchangeably with the terms sharing and onward transfer.

document-watermarking.def: A security feature that adds identifying information to downloaded documents, typically including the downloader's name or email and a timestamp. Watermarking creates an audit trail for sensitive documents and discourages unauthorized sharing.

disposal.def: A phase of the data life cycle that pertains to how an entity removes or destroys data or information.

endpoint-devices.def: Connected hardware or virtual devices that communicate across a network, such as mobile devices, laptops, desktops, and sensors.

entity.def: A legal entity or management operating model of any size established for a particular purpose. A legal entity may, for example, be a business enterprise, a not-for-profit organization, a government body, or an academic institution.

environmental.def: Of or having to do with the matters that can damage the physical elements of information systems (for example, fire, flood, wind, earthquake, power surges, or power outages).

evidence.def: An artifact demonstrating that a control operated: a report, export, configuration snapshot, screenshot, or signed document. Auditors test controls by examining evidence, so its completeness and timestamps carry the audit.

external-users.def: Users, other than entity personnel, who are authorized by entity management, customers, or other authorized persons to interact with the entity’s information system.

finding.def: A specific security observation, issue, or instance discovered during scans, assessments, or reviews. Findings may represent vulnerability instances on particular assets, misconfigurations in cloud resources, policy violations, or security gaps.

feature.def: A feature performs a specific function or capability and provides value to users. They can be basic or complex, and are designed to meet specific requirements and objectives. Features can be made available through the use of Entitlements or Feature Flags.

functional-requirements.def: Requirements that must be met for the system to correctly fulfill its designed purpose.

general-data-protection-regulation.def: A regulation established by the European Union to ensure protections for the privacy and security of personal data about individuals in the European Union.

group.def: A group is a collection of users, which may be aggregated by company, plan, or pricing tier.

governance-risk-and-compliance.def: An organization’s approach towards governance, risk management, and compliance. A company’s GRC team or responsible employees make sure that the business is on track in terms of meeting goals, operating smoothly, predicting and mitigating risks, and adhering t…

health-insurance-portability-and-account.term: Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA)
health-insurance-portability-and-account.def: A US federal law governing protected health information (PHI). Its Security Rule sets administrative, physical, and technical safeguards for electronic PHI, and its Privacy Rule governs how PHI may be used and disclosed.

hitrust.def: Many companies subject to HIPAA comply with HITRUST, an optional framework that incorporates and harmonizes requirements from HIPAA, NIST, ISO, and other standards to offer a more prescriptive and comprehensive approach to data security.

identity-holder.def: A record representing an individual affiliated with an organization, including employees and contractors.

implemented-capability.def: A technical, administrative, or physical mechanism that exists in a production environment and can demonstrate reasonable effectiveness, as distinct from one that is only planned or documented.

information-assets.def: Data and the associated software and infrastructure used to process, transmit, and store information or to produce, manufacture, or distribute products.

integrity.def: One of the Trust Services Criteria established by the AICPA, Integrity means that the data organization uses to pursue its business or keeps safe for others is reliably stored and not erased or damaged.

integration.def: A configured connection between Openlane and an external system that enables automated data synchronization and evidence collection. Integrations connect to cloud providers, security tools, identity providers, collaboration platforms, and storage services.

inclusive-method.def: A method of handling the services provided by a subservice organization in a SOC 2 report where the subservice organization's controls are included in the system description and tested by the service auditor. Contrast with the carve-out method.

infrastructure.def: The collection of physical or virtual resources that supports an overall IT environment, including the server, storage, network elements, and endpoint devices.

internal-control.def: A process, effected by an entity’s board of directors, management, and other personnel, designed to provide reasonable assurance regarding the achievement of objectives relating to operations, reporting, and compliance.

information-security.def: A set of policies or regulations put in place to safeguard a company’s data or other assets from unauthorized access or use. InfoSec regulations ensure that an organization’s sensitive information is secure.

information-security-compliance.def: InfoSec Compliance refers to ensuring that regulations and policies around information security are followed within an organization.

information-security-management-system.def: An ISMS establishes a systematic approach to managing an organization’s information security. As a documented management system, ISMS provides a set of security controls a company can record in policies, procedures, and other kinds of documents;

iso-27001-compliance.def: One of the most popular standards for Information Security ISO 27001 is often the Compliance framework of choice in the financial industry, spanning from banks, to insurance companies, and additional financial institutions.

issue.def: A risk that has been realized, or a problem that has already occurred and requires immediate attention and action.

material-control.def: A control so fundamental that no compensating control can substitute for it, and whose absence or failure could have a material impact on the organization.

material-incident.def: An incident with actual or potential material impact, whether by jeopardizing the confidentiality, integrity, availability, or safety of systems and data, or by violating organizational policy at a scale that matters.

material-risk.def: A risk whose exposure to danger, harm, or loss would have a material impact on the organization, such as significant financial damage, litigation, or safety consequences. Material risks belong in the risk register with an accountable owner.

material-threat.def: A threat vector capable of causing damage with material impact, such as nation-state operations, supply chain compromise, or poorly governed AI initiatives, documented in the organization's threat catalog.

material-weakness.def: A deficiency, or combination of control deficiencies, that makes it probable that reasonable threats will not be prevented or detected in a timely manner, undermining assurance that the organization can operate within its stated risk tolerance.

member.def: Members are people you have invited to manage your workspace at Openlane.

non-disclosure-agreement.def: A legal agreement that protects confidential information shared between parties. NDAs are commonly used between organizations and their vendors, customers, or prospects.

nist-cybersecurity-framework.def: NIST is a federal agency within the US Department of Commerce that creates guidelines, frameworks, and policies that support innovation in science and technology.

operating-effectiveness.def: Whether a control functioned as intended over a period of time (for example, throughout the period January 1 to December 31). Auditors conclude on operating effectiveness by testing a sample from the control's population;

open-source.def: Open source software is software with source code that anyone can inspect, modify, and enhance. Openlane is an example of an open-source company.

organization.def: Organizations are the highest level grouping within Openlane. Organizations are made up of users and represent a billable unit.

personal-information.def: Information that is about, or can be related to, an identifiable individual.

personal-access-token.def: A credential tied to an individual user for programmatic access. PATs follow the person: when they leave, anything relying on their tokens breaks, which is why organization-scoped API tokens are the better fit for automation. See API tokens and PATs.

platform.def: A governed system with a defined boundary: what it is, who owns it, and what sits inside and outside its scope. A SOC 2 system description is built around exactly this boundary narrative.

population.def: The number of occurrences of a control's performance during the audit period, from which the auditor samples.

policies.def: Management or board member statements of what should be done to effect control. Such statements may be documented, explicitly stated in communications, or implied through actions and decisions. Policies serve as the basis for procedures.

practitioner.def: Used when referencing AICPA procedures, a CPA who performs an examination of controls within an entity’s system relevant to security, availability, processing integrity, confidentiality, or privacy.

privacy-commitments.def: Declarations made by management regarding the performance of a system processing personal information.

privacy-notice.def: A written communication by entities that collect personal information, to the individuals about whom personal information is collected, about the entity’s (a) policies regarding the nature of the information that they will collect and how that information will…

procedure.def: The documented steps for carrying out an activity a policy requires. Policies state what must happen; procedures state how it happens, and auditors compare both against actual practice.

program.def: A container for a compliance effort with a defined goal and timeline, such as reaching SOC 2 readiness or completing an ISO 27001 certification.

project.def: A Project is a grouping inside an account, typically used to separate development and production environments or otherwise group assets for shared identification and management.

process-or-control-framework.def: A framework that contains a set of processes or controls, established by another party, that organizations are expected to implement in support of establishing an effective system of internal control.

products.def: Tangible or intangible goods manufactured or produced by an entity. Throughout this document, the term is used interchangeably with goods.

reciprocity.def: An agreement between organizations to accept each other's security assessments or assessed postures rather than re-assessing, commonly used to reuse authorizations across agencies or partners.

remediation.def: A documented action that addresses a security vulnerability or finding. Remediations include patches, configuration changes, code fixes, architecture changes, or compensating controls.

residual-risk.def: The risk to the achievement of objectives that remains after management’s response has been designed and implemented.

retention.def: A phase of the data life cycle that pertains to how long an entity stores information for future use or reference.

risk.def: A potential future event with possible negative impacts on the company's objectives. Risks may be quantified using metrics including likelihood and impact, and should be managed and treated within organizations.

risk-appetite.def: The types and amount of risk an organization is willing to accept, at a broad level, in pursuit of its objectives.

risk-register.def: The maintained list of an organization's identified risks with their scores, owners, and treatment decisions. A current register demonstrates that risk management operates as a process rather than a one-time exercise, which is what audit frameworks test for.

risk-response.def: The decision to accept, avoid, reduce, or share a risk.

risk-threshold.def: The concrete values that trigger management action or escalation when crossed, turning risk appetite and tolerance into operational decision points.

risk-tolerance.def: The level of risk an organization is willing to assume to achieve a specific result. Narrower and more operational than risk appetite.

scan.def: A systematic security assessment that examines a target for vulnerabilities, misconfigurations, or compliance gaps. Scans may be automated (scheduled vulnerability scans), on-demand (triggered by events), or manual (penetration tests).

sampling.def: Selecting a number of instances from a control's population to test its operation. The auditor's sampling methodology stipulates how many samples to select based on the population size; for example, a sample of 5 from a population of 100 terminated users.

security-event.def: An occurrence, arising from actual or attempted unauthorized access or use by internal or external parties, that impairs or could impair the availability, integrity, or confidentiality of information or systems: result in unauthorized disclosure or theft of in…

security-incident.def: A security event that requires action on the part of an entity to protect information assets and resources.

senior-management.def: The CEO or equivalent organizational leader and senior management team.

service-auditor.def: A professional accountant in public practice who, at the request of the service organization, provides an assurance report (such as a SOC 2) on controls at a service organization.

service-organization.def: A third-party organization (or segment of one) that provides services to user entities that are likely to be relevant to those user entities' control environment. In a SOC 2 engagement, the service organization is the company being audited.

service-provider.def: A supplier (such as a service organization) engaged to provide services to the entity.

security-questionnaires.def: Typically encountered in two forms: 1. Vendor Security Questionnaire, 2. Risk Assessment Questionnaire.

single-sign-on.def: Authentication delegated to a central identity provider, so people sign in once and access is granted and revoked in one place. Enforcing SSO turns offboarding from a per-application checklist into a single directory action.

soc-2-compliance.def: Applicable to all SaaS and technology companies, this audit attests that customer data is stored and managed in a secure manner.

software.def: A collection of instructions that tell a computer how to operate. Software may be both internally developed and purchased from vendors and can include both application software (for example, user applications and database management systems) and system softwar…

stakeholders.def: Parties that are affected by the entity, such as shareholders, the communities in which an entity operates, employees, customers, and suppliers.

subcontrol.def: A component of a control that is implemented and evidenced separately, used when one requirement spans several teams or systems. Splitting exposes per-component status and ownership, so a gap in one component is visible before an auditor tests the whole.

subservice-organization.def: A service organization used by another service organization to perform some of the services provided to user entities, where those services are likely to be relevant to the user entities' control environment.

subprocessor.def: A third-party vendor or service that processes personal data on behalf of an organization, extending the controller-processor chain one link further: the customer is the controller, the organization is the processor, and vendors the organization engages with t…

system.def: Refers to the infrastructure, software, procedures, and data that are designed, implemented, and operated by people to achieve one or more of the entity’s specific business objectives (for example, delivery of services or production of goods) in accordance wit…

system-description.def: The section of a SOC 2 report (Section 3) describing the policies and procedures the service organization designed and implemented to provide the services covered by the report.

system-boundaries.def: The specific aspects of an entity’s infrastructure, software, people, procedures, and data necessary to perform a function (such as producing, manufacturing, or distributing a product) or provide a service.

system-components.def: Refers to the individual elements of a system, which may be classified into the following five categories: infrastructure, software, people, processes, and data.

system-event.def: An occurrence that could lead to the loss of, or disruption to, operations, services, or functions and could result in an entity’s failure to achieve its system objectives.

system-incident.def: A system event that requires action on the part of entity management to prevent or reduce the impact of the event on the entity’s achievement of its system objectives.

system-objectives.def: The entity’s objectives, established by entity management, that are embodied in the product commitments it makes to customers, including producing or manufacturing a product that meets product performance specifications and other production, manufacturing, or…

system-requirements.def: Specifications regarding how the system should function to (a) meet the entity’s commitments to customers and others (such as customers’ customers); (b) meet the entity’s commitments to suppliers and business partners;

task.def: An individual piece of owned work with a deadline, connected to the compliance objects it serves. Tasks make follow-through auditable: the request, the owner, and the completion date live on one record instead of in email threads. In Openlane, see tasks.

third-party.def: An individual or organization other than the entity and its employees. Third parties may be customers, suppliers, business partners, or others.

threat.def: Any circumstance or event, arising from human actions or natural events, that could potentially impair (a) the achievement of an entity’s objectives, its assets, or activities of its personnel, or (b) other entities through unauthorized access, destruction, di…

third-party-risk-management.def: The methodologies used by organizations to understand and mitigate risks introduced by suppliers, partners, or other entities outside the organization.

type-i-type-ii.def: The two forms of a SOC audit. In a Type I audit, the auditor tests only the design and implementation of controls at a point in time.

trust-center.def: A customer-facing portal where organizations share their security posture, compliance certifications, and data protection practices with customers, prospects, and auditors.

trust-services-criteria.def: A set of professional attestation and advisory services based on a core set of criteria related to security, availability, processing integrity, confidentiality, or privacy.

unauthorized-access.def: Access to information or system components that (a) has not been approved by a person designated to do so by management and (b) compromises segregation of duties, confidentiality commitments, or otherwise increases risks to the information or system components…

vendor.def: An individual or business (and its employees) that is engaged to provide goods or services to the entity.

vanity-domain.def: A custom domain that an organization configures to host their Trust Center on their own branded URL (e.g., trust.yourcompany.com) instead of the default platform URL. Vanity domains require DNS configuration including CNAME and TXT records for verification.

vulnerability.def: Weakness in a component of a system, particularly information assets, system security procedures, internal controls, or implementation, that could be exploited or triggered by human action or natural events.

vulnerability-management.def: A continuous process of identifying, classifying, prioritizing, and addressing security weaknesses in systems and software.

workflow.def: An automation that acts when defined conditions are met, such as flagging records for review or routing approvals, so recurring program activity does not depend on someone remembering to initiate it.
